tier_reason: The bench code is public (benches/bench.rs and benches/real_world.rs, GEOS linked via the bench-geos-system feature, commands in docs/GEOS-SETUP.md). The Cargo bench/release profiles set lto=fat and codegen-units=1, and the CPU (i5-12400F) and GEOS 3.14.1 are stated. But no rustc version is given (only MSRV 1.88), and the 1.58M-polygon production GeoPackage is gitignored, so the headline real-world rows cannot be reproduced. That makes it first-party with partial methodology: C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (real-world table updated 2026-09-26; synthetic table refreshed 2026-09-18 from the v0.14.5 measurement set): real-world validation of 1.58M polygons 2.1 s (1.3 us/poly) vs GEOS 3.0 s (1.9 us/poly), 1.4x; full pass 3.6 s vs 3.0 s (0.83x, GEOS faster). Synthetic rows (parallel batch; ratio = GEOS/GeoRepair): valid polygon 4v 4.8x, invalid bowtie 4v 25x, invalid bowtie 1000v 8.0x, collapsed 1000v 5.5x, zero-length line 45x, zigzag ls 500v 43x, dense self ls 1000v 120x; star-burst and spoke rows reach 5632x-12573x. GEOS is faster on valid polygon 10000v (0.37x), spaghetti 500v (0.56x), large coord 1e12 1000v (0.08x), self-int ls 1000v (0.05x) and arrange valid 500v (0.25x). docs/BENCHMARKS.md (tables dated 2026-08-07): real-world validation 2.47 s vs 3.46 s (1.40x), full pass 4.05 s vs 3.49 s (0.86x). Its synthetic rows differ from the README: valid polygon 4v 2.78x, invalid bowtie 4v 21.78x, zero-length line 38.82x, valid polygon 10000v 0.31x, spaghetti 0.63-0.65x, large coord 1e12 2.38x. It says GeoRepair wins 73 of 91 cases.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust bench and release profiles: lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=unwind; mimalloc global allocator (a default feature); edition 2024, MSRV 1.88. The rustc version used for the runs is not stated. Windows x86_64. GEOS is conda-forge 3.14.1: docs/BENCHMARKS.md says an MSVC build, serial per call, no LTO, while docs/GEOS-SETUP.md calls the conda build LLVM-optimized.
corrections.caveats: Mixed results: GeoRepair loses on large valid polygons, valid linestrings of 10 or more vertices, spaghetti geometry, large coordinates, self-intersecting linestrings and the full real-world pass. The GeoRepair column is a 12-thread Rayon batch; GEOS runs serially per call but is driven concurrently through Rayon in the same process. Before 2026-08-07 the GEOS columns went through a WKT round trip that inflated wins 30-500x. The README's 2026-09-18 table still shows overlap mp 186-318x and dense grid 183-250x, while BENCHMARKS.md gives 6.85-10.34x and 4.23-13.63x for the same rows and calls ~200x figures an artifact. That contradiction is unexplained. The production GeoPackage behind the real-world rows is gitignored and not public (only benches/real_world/alaska.* is committed). The validator uses an eps-class tolerance, not GEOS exact-zero, and diverges from GEOS on 213 XML-suite cases. Line rows compare against GEOS UnaryUnion, not makeValid. The crate is labelled experimental: the latest commit (2026-09-27) fixes MultiPolygon repair output that shipped crossings. All numbers are first-party, and sub-microsecond rows are dispatch noise per the authors.

notes: The real-world numbers in the record match BENCHMARKS.md, but its synthetic ratios come from the newer README table, not BENCHMARKS.md, so I rewrote claimed_speedup to name both sources. Shortcomings worth recording: a private real-world dataset, no rustc version, and README and BENCHMARKS.md disagreeing by about 20x on the overlap and dense-grid rows. Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0, 1 star, not a fork or archived, 318 commits, last commit 2026-09-27.

tier_reason: B rests on the peer-reviewed paper 'Benchmarking and Engineering Data Structures for Spherical Range Queries' (arXiv 2607.07367). Search results list it as ESA 2026, LIPIcs DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2026.22. Its abstract (seen in search snippets) says the SPRK-tree is fastest in almost all benchmarks, and the snippets name Boost R-tree among the competitors. A public reproducibility CLI exists (wembed-pdf/rembed, reproducability branch, reproducibility-cli; Zenodo data, nix flake). The paper itself was unreachable, so its numbers, CPU and compiler were not seen and A cannot be assessed.

corrections.baseline: Boost.Geometry R-tree (named among the paper's competitors in search snippets) plus KD-trees in several languages (Kiddo, nabo, Neighbourhood), a Rust VP-tree, scikit-learn BallTree, SNN and brute force. nanoflann and CGAL kd-tree are feature-gated backends in the rembed harness, but I could not confirm they appear in the paper.
corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. The paper (arXiv 2607.07367, ESA 2026) could not be opened: arxiv.org, drops.dagstuhl.de, pith.science and api.semanticscholar.org are egress-blocked, and neither the sprk nor the rembed README quotes results. Search-result snippets of the paper (not opened) say the SPRK-tree 'consistently achieves the fastest query times in almost all benchmarks, and ranks second in the few remaining cases'. The snippets also paraphrase that at dimension 32 it is slightly faster than SNN and brute force and an order of magnitude faster than the other tree-based methods.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The sprk README advises rustflags -Ctarget-cpu=native (AVX-512 compress when available). The rembed release profile is the Cargo default plus debug=true. The paper's compiler and flags were not read.

notes: I confirmed B on the same basis as earlier batches that accepted a venue seen only in search results (auto-mpft, PowerInfer). A retier check that can open arXiv 2607.07367 should read the tables, CPU and flags (possible A, given the public reproducibility CLI) and confirm whether nanoflann, CGAL and Boost R-tree are in the results. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 3 stars, not a fork, 18 commits, last commit 2026-04-07. The repo has sprk-ffi and sprk-python directories, so C callers may be able to use it.

tier_reason: First-party Python benchmark against PyQtree, Rtree (libspatialindex) and Shapely STRtree (GEOS). The code is public (benchmarks/cross_library_bench.py with benchmarks/quadtree_bench/main.py), and the CPU (Ryzen 7 3700X) and CPython 3.14.5 are stated. Cargo.toml gives the release profile, but the rustc version is not stated, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/benchmark.md (500,000 points, 500 queries): total time fastquadtree numpy path 0.068 s (build 0.052, query 0.017), list path 0.285 s (build 0.054, query 0.231), Shapely STRtree 0.309 s (build 0.200, query 0.110), Rtree 2.351 s (build 1.805, query 0.546), PyQtree 2.909 s. That is 42.52x vs PyQtree (numpy path) and 10.20x (list path). Derived from page data: about 34.6x faster total than Rtree on the numpy path and 8.2x on the list path; against Shapely STRtree, 4.5x total on the numpy path but only 1.08x on the list path, and STRtree's query time (0.110 s) beats the list path's (0.231 s). The drop-in pyqtree shim takes 1.127 s vs 11.647 s for the original pyqtree (10.333x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CPython 3.14.5. The Rust engine is built via PyO3/maturin with a Cargo.toml release profile of opt-level=3, lto=thin, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. The rustc version is not stated (MSRV 1.89).
corrections.caveats: First-party Python benchmark. The best number uses the numpy return path; the list path, which is comparable to Rtree's list returns, is much slower and loses to Shapely STRtree on query time. The Shapely STRtree row uses numpy points and returns. Both sides include Python call overhead, and Rtree inserts go one at a time through ctypes. The rustc version is not stated. Only 500 queries are run, on uniform point data rather than extended geometries.

notes: Every number in the record matches docs/benchmark.md (the README carries the same table). I added the Shapely STRtree comparison, the only native incumbent that is close: fastquadtree wins only on the numpy path. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 33 stars, 2 forks, not a fork or archived, 303 commits, last commit 2026-06-22.
